passage:
Counselling session note. Pooja Sethi, workplace wellbeing service, Tuesday
Irfan (25, software developer) came in agitated. His batchmate Arvind launched a small budgeting app last month. Irfan called it "buggy, ugly, with a typo on the home screen", and said it already has thousands of users and a write-up in a tech newsletter.
Irfan has been building his own app for eighteen months and has not shown it to anyone. "It isn't ready," he said. Then, quietly: "I'm so jealous I can't sleep. And I don't understand. He broke every rule."
When I asked which rules, he listed them: no bugs at launch, perfect design, nothing shown until it is finished. After a pause he said, "Who made those rules? Nobody told me them. I think I made them."
He looked ashamed and a little lighter at the same time.
Plan: next session, explore what a "good enough" first release could look like. Check in on sleep.

qa.q: How long has Irfan been building his own app?
qa.a: For eighteen months.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Irfan show about Arvind's success?
qa.a: Envy that keeps him awake, confusion that imperfect work succeeded and shame at being stuck, with some lightness as he sees the rules were his own.

qa.q: What next step does the counsellor plan, and why does it fit this stage?
qa.a: Exploring what a 'good enough' first release could look like, which builds on Irfan's own insight that his strict rules were self-made.

qa.q: How might Arvind see his own launch, compared with how Irfan sees it?
qa.a: Arvind may see it as a rough first version worth improving with users, while Irfan sees mainly the bugs and the typo.

grounding: Shows a developer's envy, confusion and shame on seeing a peer succeed with imperfect work, and his dawning sense that his perfect-launch rules were his own.

passage:
Sunday night
Vishal from art school got his first gallery show. I saw the poster today, then went and looked at his work online, and I'm still sitting with it.
The paintings are... fine. Loose. One hand is clearly wrong. He has posted every single piece since college, even the bad ones: sketches, half-finished things. And people love it. The gallery owner found him through those posts.
I have forty-one canvases in Nani's storeroom, and I have never shown one. Every single one needed "one more layer".
I'm so jealous it made my face hot. Then ashamed of being jealous. Then confused. I always thought the rule was: only show it when it's flawless. But Vishal never followed that rule, and the world didn't punish him. So whose rule was it?
Maybe mine. Maybe only ever mine.
Rajni

qa.q: How many canvases does Rajni have in Nani's storeroom?
qa.a: Forty-one canvases.

qa.q: What feelings did seeing Vishal's show bring up for Rajni?
qa.a: Jealousy that made Rajni's face hot, then shame about the jealousy, then confusion about the rule of only showing flawless work.

qa.q: What small experiment could Rajni try next?
qa.a: Rajni could show one canvas, even one that 'needs one more layer', to a trusted friend or online, and notice what actually happens.

qa.q: How might Vishal think about posting his bad sketches?
qa.a: Vishal seems to treat rough pieces as part of the journey worth sharing, not as failures to hide.

grounding: Illustrates envy, shame and confusion at a peer succeeding with imperfect work, and the painter beginning to see the flawless-only rule as self-made.

passage:
In the small town of Dharwad, Raghav had been working on his handmade-furniture website for a year. It still wasn't live. The photos weren't perfect. The descriptions needed another edit.
Then his old classmate Madhuri messaged: "My shop page just got its hundredth order!" He looked. Her photos were blurry. One description had a spelling mistake. And she was succeeding.
Raghav felt a hot wave of envy, then confusion. How? Then shame. A year, and nothing to show.
That night he lay awake. Who had told him everything had to be perfect before launching? Nobody, he realised. That rule had been his own all along.

qa.q: How long had Raghav been working on his website?
qa.a: A year.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Raghav have looking at Madhuri's page?
qa.a: He felt envy, then confusion, then shame at being stuck for a year while she succeeded with imperfect work.

qa.q: What turning point does Raghav reach at night?
qa.a: He realises the perfection rule was his own, not the world's, which opens the way to launching.

qa.q: How might Madhuri feel if she knew Raghav was envious?
qa.a: Madhuri might feel surprised, since she knows her page isn't perfect, and perhaps want to encourage him.

grounding: Shows a young man seeing a peer succeed with imperfect work, feeling envy, confusion and shame, and realising his rules were his own.

passage:
In Lagos, Nkechi had been planning her baking business for two years: the logo, the menu, the perfect photos. Nothing had launched.
At a friend's wedding, she met Alejandro, a university friend visiting from Madrid. He'd started a small food stall six months ago. "The first month was a disaster," he laughed. "Burnt everything. But now I have regulars."
Nkechi smiled, but inside something twisted. Envy. Confusion. He'd started with burnt food and a messy stall, and he was doing fine. She had two years of perfect plans and nothing to show.
On the drive home, the shame burned. Then a quieter thought: nobody had ever told her she had to be perfect first. She had told herself.

qa.q: How long had Alejandro's food stall been running?
qa.a: Six months.

qa.q: What was Nkechi feeling as Alejandro laughed about the disaster?
qa.a: She felt envy and confusion, and then shame at having nothing to show after two years.

qa.q: What realisation opens a new path for Nkechi?
qa.a: That the rule of being perfect first was her own, not the world's, so she could start imperfectly.

qa.q: How might Alejandro see his own messy start?
qa.a: Alejandro seems relaxed and amused about it, seeing the mistakes as part of getting going.

grounding: Shows a young woman seeing a peer succeed after a messy start, feeling envy, confusion and shame, and realising her rules were her own.

passage:
At the design studio's Friday review, Bidisha watched Yogesh present his app prototype. Rough edges. Placeholder text. A button in the wrong colour.
The client loved it. "Ship it. We'll improve as we go."
Bidisha had been polishing her own prototype for six weeks. It still wasn't ready to show.
She felt something bitter rise in her throat. Envy. And confusion: why did his messy work get praised? Then shame, sitting heavily in her chest. Six weeks, and nothing shown.
At her desk afterwards, she stared at her perfect, unseen prototype and asked herself: whose rule was it that nothing could be shown until it was flawless? Not the client's, clearly.

qa.q: How long had Bidisha been polishing her prototype?
qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling as the client praised Yogesh's prototype?
qa.a: She felt envy, confusion about why his rough work was praised, and shame at having nothing to show.

qa.q: What turning point is Bidisha approaching at her desk?
qa.a: Seeing that the rule of showing only flawless work was hers, not the client's, so she could share her prototype sooner.

qa.q: How might Yogesh feel about his rough prototype being approved?
qa.a: Yogesh probably feels pleased and relaxed, comfortable improving as he goes.

grounding: Shows a designer watching a peer's rough work succeed, feeling envy, confusion and shame, and questioning her own rules.

passage:
Pradeep,
I saw your launch post. Congratulations, truly. And I have to be honest about what I felt, because it surprised me.
Envy first. Then confusion. Your app has a typo on the login screen, two of the promised features aren't there yet, and a thousand people signed up in a week anyway. Meanwhile my recipe site has been "almost ready" for fourteen months because the photos aren't perfect.
I felt ashamed sitting there, stuck, while you were out in the world with a typo.
Then a strange thought: who told me it had to be perfect? Not the users. Not you. Not any rule I can find. I made that rule up, and I've been obeying it like law.
Can I show you the site this weekend, as it is? Tell me the three worst things. I think I'm ready to hear them.
Sharmila

qa.q: How long has Sharmila's recipe site been "almost ready"?
qa.a: Fourteen months.

qa.q: What did Sharmila feel on seeing Pradeep's launch?
qa.a: Envy first, then confusion, then shame at being stuck while Pradeep shipped imperfect work.

qa.q: What step is Sharmila taking, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Offering to show the site as it is and hear the three worst things, testing the self-made perfection rule against real feedback.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel reading this email?
qa.a: Pradeep may feel touched by the honesty and glad to help, perhaps amused that a typo started it all.

grounding: Shows a person seeing a peer succeed with imperfect work, feeling envy, confusion and shame, and realising the perfection rule was self-made.
